title: Who made, sold, relabelled and collected the slide? Attribution layers in the nineteenth-century slide trade
research_problem: A commercial microscope slide can accumulate several names and numbers. Maker/preparator, wholesaler, retailer, later dealer, collector and museum may each leave a label or address. Treating the most visible label as a single 'maker' field destroys transaction history.
core_rule: Never collapse maker/preparator, seller/retailer, later relabeller, collector number and current accession into one creator field unless the historical evidence explicitly identifies them as the same actor.

norman_case.repository: University of St Andrews Libraries and Museums — Bell Pettigrew slide collection
documented_trade_structure: Norman's only catalogue appeared in 1872 and listed 2,584 mounts without prices.
Slides carrying the J. T. Norman name continued to be made after Norman's death under the original business name.
The institution states that Norman supplied well-known mounters including Richard Suter, who may have sold slides under their own labels.
Microscope makers and suppliers also bought Norman slides and examples with secondary labels survive.
norman_case.research_consequence: A slide labelled Norman can indicate maker/business identity, while an overlying or secondary supplier label can indicate a distinct retail transaction. The reverse is also possible: a Norman retail label need not prove Norman prepared the specimen if the business resold other material.
norman_case.guard: Do not date a Norman-name slide solely from the founder's lifetime; business-name persistence is explicitly documented.

buyer_cabinet_implication.claim: Private cabinets should be treated as transaction residues containing heterogeneous maker-retailer histories, not as coherent maker collections unless proven.
examples: Manchester Gibson cabinet: many supplier/maker/locality/date labels within numbered trays.
Whipple Pritchard-labelled cabinet: commercial slides coexist with homemade and broken preparations.
Fred Enock personal collection at auction: Enock's own work coexisted with slides by Elcock, Norman, Topping, Watson and others.

workflow: Photograph/transcribe every label separately and preserve physical layering/order.
Identify maker/preparator only from maker mark, catalogue match, archival attribution or strong material/label evidence.
Identify retailer/agent independently from seller labels and addresses.
Record collector marks/numbers as a separate namespace even when identity is unknown.
Then search historical maker catalogues using exact subject wording.
Only after the object layers are established should price/format rows be attached.
research_payoff: The slide trade was not a simple maker-to-buyer line. A single object could pass through manufacture, wholesale/retail relabelling, private re-numbering, resale and museum accession while retaining multiple labels. Those accretions are evidence of circulation rather than cataloguing noise.
